name: African socialism
info: African socialism is a family of socialist theories developed in post-colonial Africa from the mid-20th century, built on the claim that traditional African communities are naturally socialist, and it shaped the policies of Tanzania, Ghana, Senegal and other states.

facts.thinkers: Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, author of Ujamaa; Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, whose philosophy is called Nkrumahism; Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, poet of the Négritude movement; Abdoulaye Ly, whose 1956 book was the first influential socialist text tailored for Africa; Sékou Touré of Guinea and Modibo Keïta of Mali; Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu, who echoed its themes
facts.texts: Abdoulaye Ly's Les masses africaines et l'actuelle condition humaine (1956); the Arusha Declaration (1967); Nkrumah's A declaration to the colonial peoples; Senghor's The Challenge of Culture in French West Africa and Vues sur l'Afrique noire, ou s'assimiler, non être assimilés; William H. Friedland and Carl G. Rosberg Jr., eds., African Socialism
facts.ideas: traditional African communities as naturally socialist; a classless pre-colonial society; social development led by a large public sector; an emphasis on African identity; political and economic autonomy and self-reliance; Africanisation of business and the civil service; Pan-Africanism and non-alignment
facts.today: Ujamaa and Nyerere have seen a resurgence in popularity in Tanzania since his death; Senegal's Socialist Party, founded by Senghor, is part of the movement's record; Ubuntu and Harambee, the related ideas of South Africa and Kenya, remain in use as terms of community

t: African socialism holds that traditional African cultures and community structures lean naturally toward socialism, so that Africa needed no class struggle and its socialism differs from Marxism and European socialist theory.

Several African countries adopted socialist systems from the 1950s to the mid-1980s, about 35 of the 50 to 53 countries of the time, and Ghana, Guinea, Senegal and Tanzania took it as a model of economic development.

Tanzania's Ujamaa villagisation of 1968 to 1975 fell short of its goals, which the general international consensus attributes to its accelerated timeline and bureaucratic inefficiency, though by the end of Nyerere's term 96% of children had gone to primary school.
dyk: Senghor answered a question about nationalising French companies in Senegal by saying that it would be to "kill the goose that laid the golden egg", and Senegal kept the French franc as its currency.
ev: Abdoulaye Ly publishes Les masses africaines et l'actuelle condition humaine, the first influential socialist text tailored for Africa
Nkrumah helps found the Union of Independent African States of Ghana, Mali and Guinea; Senegal votes 97% for association with France in the referendum
Senegal becomes independent and Léopold Senghor is elected its president
Senegal's Socialist Party is declared the country's only legal party
Julius Nyerere issues the Arusha Declaration, committing Tanzania to a socialist reform programme built on Ujamaa
Tanzania begins consolidating its rural population into village communities, a programme that runs to 1975
Tanzania commits to a National Economic Survival Programme of policy changes to liberalise its economy
Nyerere steps down from the presidency of Tanzania

sections.origins:
African socialism is a distinct variant of socialist theory developed in post-colonial Africa during the mid-20th century. As many African countries gained independence during the 1960s, some of the new governments rejected capitalism in favour of a more Afrocentric economic model, and their leaders professed that they were practising African socialism. It is a shared ideology among several African thinkers that encompasses a variety of competing interpretations.

The first influential publication of socialist thought tailored for application in Africa was Les masses africaines et l'actuelle condition humaine (1956) by the Senegalese intellectual Abdoulaye Ly. The defining theme running through the different theories is the notion that traditional African cultures and community structures have a natural inclination toward socialist principles. This characterisation of socialism as an indigenous African tradition set the movement apart from other socialist movements on the continent and elsewhere.

According to William H. Friedland and Carl G. Rosberg Jr., the editors of the book African Socialism, its main architects were Julius Nyerere in Tanzania, Léopold Senghor in Senegal, Joseph Saidu Momoh and Siaka Stevens in Sierra Leone, Kwame Nkrumah and Hilla Limann in Ghana, François Tombalbaye in Chad, Modibo Keïta in Mali, Sékou Touré in Guinea and Luís Cabral in Guinea-Bissau.
sections.ideas:
The common principles of the various versions were social development guided by a large public sector, an emphasis on African identity and on the meaning of being African, and the preservation or revival of a classless society. Senghor claimed that "Africa's social background of tribal community life not only makes socialism natural to Africa but excludes the validity of the theory of class struggle", which made African socialism, in all its variations, different from Marxism and European socialist theory.

Nyerere's framework was Ujamaa, Swahili for "familyhood", meant to join traditional communal values to modern economic and social development. He saw it as distinct from the Marxist tradition: its goal was the restoration of the pre-colonial family unit, in which members of a larger familial network support each other and share work. Ujamaa was not meant to replace a failing capitalist system but to deconstruct the artificial power structures imposed by colonial rule. Nyerere held that in indigenous African culture nobody starved, for food or of human dignity, for lack of personal wealth, since he could depend on his community. The ideal society would rest on "freedom, equality, and unity".

African socialists argued for a distinctive form of socialism because they believed it had its roots in pre-colonial African society, which they described as classless, communal, and democratic through government by discussion and consensus. Nelson Mandela likewise asserted that in the past in Africa there were no classes and no exploitation of man by man.
sections.spread:
African socialism became an important model of economic development for Ghana, Guinea, Senegal and Tanzania. These countries used different models, but many commonalities emerged: the desire for political and economic autonomy, self-reliance, the Africanisation of business and the civil service, Pan-Africanism and non-alignment. Several African countries adopted socialist systems from the 1950s to the mid-1980s, roughly 35 of the 50 to 53 countries at the time.

Other local ideas are linked with it. Ubuntu, from the Zulu and Xhosa languages, recognises the humanity of a person through their relationships with others; Archbishop Desmond Tutu described the person with ubuntu as open and accessible to others. Harambee, a word that originated among Swahili porters of East Africa and means "let us pull together", was taken in Kenya as an opportunity for local communities to develop themselves without waiting for government; analysts state that it also brought class discrepancies, because some individuals used it to generate wealth.

Nkrumah pushed Ghana to become an international advocate of socialism and Pan-Africanism, and in 1958 he helped found the Union of Independent African States of Ghana, Mali and Guinea. The union was short-lived, but it marked the first attempt at regional unity among the newly established African republics.
sections.power:
In Ghana, Nkrumah began infrastructure and economic plans after independence in 1957, including $16 million for a new town at Tema as a seaport for Accra, and thousands of new rural schools. His government slowly increased the number of state-controlled firms and restricted privately owned companies. By 1965 the state controlled 50% of the insurance industry, 60% of bank deposits were in state banks, and the state handled 35% of imports. He turned toward the Communist powers, visiting Moscow in 1961; in 1963 he told a Soviet delegation in Accra that Ghana had chosen the socialist path.

In Tanzania the Arusha Declaration of 1967 committed the country to socialist reform. From 1968 to 1975 Nyerere's government consolidated rural Tanzania into village-style agricultural communities where resources were to be shared. Most of these communities did not become self-sufficient, and much production stayed on independent small farms. The forced collectivisation of land that had been family-owned was a sore point for many farmers. Some historians describe the state's control over village management and production, which grew from a voluntary and decentralised start, as coercive and autocratic.

In Senegal, Senghor led a moderated version. The 1958 referendum, a failed coup by his Prime Minister in 1962 and a vote of 99% to abolish that post strengthened the presidency; in 1966 the Socialist Party became the only legal party. Senegal kept the French franc and French advisors and companies, invested in education and the public sector, and protected peanut prices.
sections.critiques:
The general international consensus is that Ujamaa failed to live up to its goals. The accelerated timeline of the reforms and bureaucratic inefficiency led to disappointing economic results, and the state's focus on agricultural production inhibited its ability to address socioeconomic class division in the cities. Some historians have labelled the state's control over villages coercive and autocratic and argued that it contradicted the democratic values Ujamaa espoused. A backlash in the late 1970s and 1980s followed, and Tanzania liberalised its economy from 1981.

Soviet Africanists disputed the idea. In the early 1960s Ivan Potekhin argued that African socialism could not exist because there could be no varieties of true Marxist-Leninist socialism, and Soviet specialists did not agree that African society had been classless. They believed Africa could have its own road to socialism but not its own form of it. They counted Guinea, Mali and Ghana as closer to Marxist-Leninist socialism, and Touré (1961), Keïta (1963) and Nkrumah (1962) received Lenin Peace Prizes; Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire were considered reactionary and prone to collaboration with imperialist powers.

On women, the record is mixed. In Ghana and Tanzania gender hierarchies persisted, and in Senegal the Code de la Famille and a set of quotas in the 1980s were more the result of male political competition than of women's movements. Many Tanzanian women nonetheless recall villagisation positively, as it let them live closer to kin.
sections.legacy:
Ujamaa has been praised for linking economic development and social liberation, a connection that anticipated a framework which did not become mainstream in Western sociology until the late 20th century. By the end of Nyerere's tenure 96% of children had gone to primary school, 50% of them girls; female life expectancy had risen from 41 to 50.7 years between 1960 and 1980, and maternal mortality had fallen from 450 per 100,000 births to under 200 by 1973.

Nyerere stepped down in 1985 but continued to advocate his model of socialism until his death. Since then he and Ujamaa have seen a resurgence in popularity in Tanzania. Ujamaa had also tied its aims to resisting Western-controlled international economic institutions: Nyerere claimed that true liberation from colonialism required Tanzania to be economically self-sufficient, with its farming villages at the heart of that development.

Senghor's career shows another strand. A leading figure of the Négritude movement, which informed his politics, he published Chants d'ombre in 1945 and the Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malagache in 1948, and hoped Négritude would represent the sum total of the values of the civilisation of the African world. As president he later liberalised the election laws to allow a three-party system of one socialist, one liberal and one communist party.

summary: African socialism is a set of post-colonial theories holding that traditional African communities are naturally socialist and classless. Nyerere's Ujamaa, Nkrumah's Nkrumahism and Senghor's moderate socialism shaped policy in Tanzania, Ghana and Senegal, with mixed results.
notes: Start 1956, circa true: the article says only 'mid-20th century' and dates the first influential publication (Ly) to 1956. The Arusha Declaration is 1967.
End null: the article treats the socialist systems as running 'from the 1950s to mid-1980s' but also reports a resurgence of Ujamaa in Tanzania; editor may prefer an end of c. 1985.
The article spells Nkrumah's era 'by 1965' figures but gives no sources; kept as given. The $16 million for Tema is given without a year.

Article contradiction: it says Nyerere's 'forced collectivization' and also that Ujamaa was 'voluntary, decentralized' at the outset, and calls the failure 'the general international consensus'; kept as attributed. The 'Ghana, Mali and Guinea' union is dated 1958; the article says Ghana was the first colonial state independent, 1957.

The article's 'Women and African socialism' section is garbled in places (eastern European comparison, feminist conferences); only its clearer points are used. Its account of Ghana's 1980s women's land is left out.
The Anthologie title is spelt 'malagache' in the article; kept as the article spells it.

Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu are listed as thinkers only as the article quotes them, not as architects. Ubuntu and Harambee are described as the article does; the article does not itself say they are part of African socialism beyond giving them subsections.
Left out: the Tanzanian Nyerere quotation in full, Kenya details beyond Harambee, Sierra Leone, Chad, Guinea-Bissau (named only as architects).
